topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

outline.topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as a Function
sections.content: Establish that a matrix isn't just a grid of numbers, but a 'machine' that moves space. Introduce the concept of basis vectors (i-hat and j-hat) on a 2D coordinate grid and how a matrix tracks where they land.
sections.example: Visualizing 'Robo-Cat' standing on a unit square. A matrix A moves Robo-Cat’s feet (i-hat) and head (j-hat) to new coordinates, effectively stretching or rotating the character.

sections.title: Step 1: The First Transformation (Rotation)
sections.content: Introduce the first linear transformation, Matrix A. Explain that applying A to a vector x results in a new vector Ax. Graphically show the entire grid warping under this single rule.
sections.example: Matrix A is a '90-degree Rotation Ray'. When fired at Robo-Cat, he rotates from standing upright to lying on his side. We denote this state as Vector v' = A * v.

sections.title: Step 2: The Second Transformation (Shear)
sections.content: Introduce a second transformation, Matrix B, which acts on the *result* of the first transformation. This demonstrates the sequential nature of operations.
sections.example: Matrix B is a 'Horizontal Shear Device'. We apply it to the already-rotated Robo-Cat. Now, Robo-Cat is not only on his side but also leaning forward. This final state is Vector v'' = B * (A * v).

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: Composition via Multiplication
sections.content: Explain that instead of applying two matrices one after the other, we can find a single 'Master Matrix' C that performs both steps in one jump. This Master Matrix is the product BA.
sections.example: An animation shows two paths: the two-step process (Rotate then Shear) vs. a single direct jump. The direct jump is the 'Composition Ray' C, where C = B × A. Emphasize that the order is right-to-left because A happens first.

sections.title: Mechanics: Why the Dot Product Works
sections.content: Briefly connect the visual composition to the numerical calculation. Show that the columns of the product matrix are simply the result of Matrix B acting on the columns of Matrix A.
sections.example: Highlight the first column of Matrix A (where i-hat landed). Multiply Matrix B by this column. The result is the first column of Matrix C. Visually, we are tracking where the 'original' ground (i-hat) ends up after both transformations.

sections.title: Summary & Order Sensitivity
sections.content: Wrap up by reinforcing that matrix multiplication is non-commutative (AB ≠ BA) because the order of actions matters in the physical world.
sections.example: Show that 'Shearing then Rotating' Robo-Cat results in a different final position than 'Rotating then Shearing' him. This proves why the order of matrix multiplication is critical for reaching the correct destination.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Matrix as a Function
lecture_lines: A matrix is a function that moves space.
We track basis vectors i-hat and j-hat.
[Asset: Robo-Cat] stands on the initial unit square.
The matrix maps basis vectors to new positions.
This transformation stretches or rotates the entire space.
animations: Fade in a dark gray (#333333) coordinate grid on a black background.
Draw red (#FF0000) vector i-hat and green (#00FF00) vector j-hat at (1,0) and (0,1).
Place Robo-Cat figure on the unit square bounded by the basis vectors.
Warp the grid smoothly so i-hat moves to (1,1) and j-hat moves to (-1,1).
Display Matrix A [[1, -1], [1, 1]] with columns colored red and green.

storyboard.title: Step 1: The First Transformation (Rotation)
lecture_lines: Matrix A acts as a ninety-degree rotation.
[Asset: Robo-Cat] rotates from upright to his side.
Vector v becomes v-prime after this transformation.
animations: Show Robo-Cat upright on a standard grid (#333333).
Display blue (#4488FF) rotation matrix A [[0, -1], [1, 0]] on screen.
Rotate the grid and Robo-Cat 90 degrees counter-clockwise smoothly.

storyboard.title: Step 2: The Second Transformation (Shear)
lecture_lines: Now apply Matrix B, a horizontal shear device.
It acts on the already rotated vector result.
[Asset: Robo-Cat] is now both rotated and leaning.
animations: Start with the rotated grid and Robo-Cat from the previous state.
Display orange (#FF8844) shear matrix B [[1, 1], [0, 1]] on screen.
Apply horizontal shear to the already rotated grid and Robo-Cat.

storyboard.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: Composition via Multiplication
lecture_lines: One 'Master Matrix' can perform both steps instantly.
This single jump is the composition of transformations.
We calculate Matrix C by multiplying B and A.
Order is right-to-left because A occurs first.
Composition C equals B times A for direct movement.
animations: Show the original grid and final sheared-rotated grid side-by-side.
Animate a ghost Robo-Cat performing rotation (A) then shear (B).
Animate a solid Robo-Cat jumping directly to the final state.
Display yellow (#FFFF00) equation C = B * A on the screen.
Flash Matrix A then Matrix B in the equation to emphasize order.

storyboard.title: Mechanics: Why the Dot Product Works
lecture_lines: Matrix B acts on the columns of Matrix A.
We track the final destination of original basis vectors.
This links visual motion to the numerical dot product.
animations: Highlight the transformed i-hat vector from Matrix A in red (#FF0000).
Show orange matrix B (#FF8844) multiplying this red vector visually.
Move the resulting vector into the first column of the product matrix C.

storyboard.title: Summary & Order Sensitivity
lecture_lines: Order matters because matrix multiplication is non-commutative.
Shearing then rotating yields a different final result.
[Asset: Robo-Cat] reaches a unique position for each order.
This proves that A-B does not equal B-A.
Sequential actions in space are order-dependent.
animations: Show two grids side-by-side with Robo-Cat on each grid.
Animate Sequence BA on the left and Sequence AB on the right.
Highlight the different final positions of Robo-Cat on each grid.
Display 'A * B is not equal to B * A' in bold white (#FFFFFF).
Fade out everything except the text 'Order Matters in Composition'.
